quick: 750 mg IV x2 doses >=7 days apart (>=50 kg)
Indicated in non-dialysis CKD; no dose change
No specific adjustment; avoid iron overload
Serum phosphate, Hb, iron indices, BP, hypersensitivity
summary: Ferric carboxymaltose (Injectafer) is an IV iron-carbohydrate complex for iron deficiency anemia in patients intolerant of or unresponsive to oral iron, in non-dialysis CKD, and for iron deficiency in NYHA II/III heart failure. Given as two 750 mg doses at least 7 days apart (>=50 kg) or 15 mg/kg (<50 kg). Key risks are hypersensitivity (including anaphylaxis), symptomatic hypophosphatemia, and transient hypertension.
indications: Iron deficiency anemia in adults and pediatric patients >=1 year with intolerance or unsatisfactory response to oral iron
Iron deficiency anemia in adults with non-dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease
Iron deficiency in adults with NYHA class II/III heart failure to improve exercise capacity

dosage.d: 750 mg IV per dose; cumulative 1,500 mg of iron per course
dosage.n: May repeat course if IDA recurs

dosage.d: 15 mg/kg up to maximum 1,000 mg IV
Per Table 1 of label (by body weight <70 vs >=70 kg and Hb)
dosage.n: NYHA II/III to improve exercise capacity

admin: Administer IV as slow push at ~100 mg (2 mL)/min or as infusion diluted in up to 250 mL 0.9% NaCl (concentration not below 2 mg iron/mL)
Infuse over at least 15 minutes when given as infusion
Avoid extravasation - causes persistent brown skin staining; stop infusion immediately if it occurs
Observe for hypersensitivity during and for at least 30 minutes after each administration until clinically stable
Only give where personnel and resuscitation/anaphylaxis therapies are immediately available
moa: Ferric carboxymaltose is a colloidal iron (III) hydroxide complexed with carboxymaltose, a carbohydrate polymer. The complex is taken up by the reticuloendothelial system where it dissociates to release iron, which is then incorporated into ferritin/transferrin and delivered to the bone marrow for incorporation into hemoglobin, replenishing depleted iron stores.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to ferric carboxymaltose or any component
relative: Anemia not due to iron deficiency
monitor: Patients at risk for hypophosphatemia (repeat courses, malnutrition, vitamin D deficiency, hyperparathyroidism)
Prior hypersensitivity to other parenteral iron

preg: Parenteral iron may cause hypersensitivity reactions with serious fetal consequences such as fetal bradycardia. Avoid in the first trimester; if needed, use in the 2nd/3rd trimester when benefit justifies risk. Untreated maternal iron deficiency anemia also carries risk. Monitor the fetus during administration after the first trimester.
lact: Iron is present in human milk in small amounts; passage of ferric carboxymaltose into breast milk is minimal and considered compatible with breastfeeding. Consider monitoring breastfed infants for GI effects (constipation, diarrhea).
renal: Indicated for IDA in adults with non-dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease; no specific dose adjustment required. Renal elimination of iron is negligible.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment provided. Use with caution and avoid in iron overload; assess iron status to prevent accumulation in hepatic dysfunction.

moderate: Oral iron preparations - reduced oral iron absorption; withhold oral iron during parenteral therapy
Other parenteral iron products - additive risk of iron overload
interactions.alcohol: No clinically significant interaction with alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: May transiently elevate serum ferritin and cause large transient elevations of serum iron; serum iron testing within 24 hours may overestimate iron. May cause asymptomatic transaminase elevations and reduce serum phosphate.

serious: Symptomatic hypophosphatemia with osteomalacia and fractures (repeat courses)
rare: Persistent brown skin staining from extravasation
emergency: Anaphylaxis (hypotension, wheezing, collapse, loss of consciousness)

monitoring: Hemoglobin and iron indices (ferritin, transferrin saturation) for response before re-dosing
Serum phosphate in patients at risk who require a repeat course
Blood pressure during and after each administration
Signs/symptoms of hypersensitivity for at least 30 minutes post-dose
counsel: This is an IV iron given as a short course; stop oral iron during treatment unless told otherwise
Report any rash, itching, wheeze, dizziness or swelling during or after the infusion immediately
Report bone or muscle pain, weakness or fatigue which may signal low phosphate
Temporary flushing, mild headache or dizziness can occur
A brownish skin mark can occur if the medicine leaks at the injection site
pk: Reticulocyte rise within days; Hb rise over 1-2 weeks
Serum iron 15 min to ~1.2 h after dose
Iron stores replenished over weeks; effect lasts months
Store 20-25 C (68-77 F); do not freeze
pearls: High-dose IV iron: up to 1,000-1,500 mg of iron per course, far more than older agents
Symptomatic hypophosphatemia is a characteristic class effect, more common than with most other IV irons - check phosphate before repeat courses
Test-dose not required, but observe >=30 min for hypersensitivity
Useful in non-dialysis CKD and NYHA II/III heart failure to improve exercise capacity
Extravasation leaves long-lasting brown skin staining - secure the line and stop at first sign of leakage
missed: Not patient-administered; each dose is given by a healthcare provider. If a scheduled second dose is delayed, complete the course as directed once at least 7 days have elapsed from the prior dose; reassess iron status and hemoglobin before re-dosing.
overdose: Excessive dosing can cause iron accumulation/overload (hemosiderosis). Do not administer to patients with iron overload. Treat overload symptomatically; consider iron chelation (e.g., deferoxamine) for clinically significant accumulation. Monitor ferritin and transferrin saturation.
